UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS

UNITED STATES OF AMERICA,

v.
STATE OF CALIFORNIA; SHIRLEY 
WEBER, PH.D., in her official capacity as 
the California Secretary of State; DEAN 
LOGAN, in his official capacity as the 
County of Los Angeles RegistrarRecorder/County Clerk,
Defendants – Appellees,
SERVICES, IMMIGRANT RIGHTS AND 
EDUCATION NETWORK; MI FAMILIA 
EN ACCION; LEAGUE OF UNITED 
LATIN AMERICAN CITIZENS; 
NATIONAL ASSOCIATION FOR THE 
ADVANCEMENT OF COLORED 
PEOPLE; CALIFORNIA-HAWAII STATE 
CONFERENCE OF THE NATIONAL 
ASSOCIATION FOR THE 
ADVANCEMENT OF COLORED 
PEOPLE,

No. 26-7231
D.C. No.
2:26-cv-12025-DOC-ADSCentral
District of California,
Los Angeles
ORDER
Before: Mark J. Bennett, Patrick J. Bumatay, and Gabriel P. Sanchez, Circuit Judges
FILED
OCT 30 2026
MOLLY C. DWYER, CLERK
U.S. COURT OF APPEALS
(1a)

2
PER CURIAM:
Dissent by Judge BUMATAY.
The United States sued the State of California and the County of Los Angeles 
(the “County”)1(collectively, “Defendants”), alleging that the Supremacy Clause 
prohibits Defendants from knowingly sending vote-by-mail ballots to individuals 
the federal government has identified as “likely” noncitizens and counting those 
ballots in violation of 18 U.S.C. § 611. The district court denied the United States’s 
application for a temporary restraining order (“TRO”), and the United States 
appeals. Presently before us is the United States’s emergency motion for an
injunction pending appeal.
2
 We deny the United States’s motion because the United 
States has failed to meet its burden in showing that an injunction pending appeal is 
warranted.
I.
Over the summer months of 2026, the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration 
Services and the Department of Homeland Security Investigations obtained 
California’s voter roll and curated a list of “high-confidence” noncitizens who they 
1 The United States sued Shirley N. Weber, in her official capacity as the California 
Secretary of State, and Dean C. Logan, in his official capacity as the County of Los 
Angeles – Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk. 
2 The United States has asked us to expedite ruling and to rule by October 30, 2026. 
We do so.
2a

3
believed were registered to vote in California. On October 12, 2026, the United 
States provided the list (“October List”) to Defendants and asked them to sequester
the ballots of every name on the list so that the voters’ citizenships could be verified 
before the votes were separated from their envelopes and counted in the November 
3, 2026, election. Defendants refused, expressing doubt about the veracity and 
reliability of the list. The United States sued Defendants on October 15, 2026, 
approximately two weeks before the 2026 midterm election, alleging that the 
Supremacy Clause prohibits Defendants from knowingly sending vote-by-mail 
ballots to likely noncitizens and counting those ballots. The United States claimed 
that these acts would violate 18 U.S.C. § 611. The United States moved for a TRO 
and appealed when the district court failed to rule on the TRO by a deadline the
United States set for the court to rule.
On appeal, the United States asked us for emergency relief in the form of a
mandatory injunction ordering Defendants to “(1) to set aside vote-by-mail ballots 
from persons identified by the Federal Government likely to be noncitizens and (2) 
to independently—or in collaboration with the Federal Government—verify their 
citizenship status before tabulating their vote-by-mail ballot.” United States v. 
California, No. 26-7070, 2026 WL 3212945, at *1 (9th Cir. Oct. 26, 2026)
(“California I”) (per curiam). We held that we lacked jurisdiction over the appeal, 
3a

4
granted the County’s motion to dismiss the appeal, and denied as moot the United 
States’s emergency motion for relief. Id.
The district court then held a hearing on the TRO application on October 27, 
2026. The next day, the district court issued an order denying the TRO. The United 
States immediately appealed and filed the instant emergency motion for an 
injunction pending appeal on October 29, 2026. The emergency motion seeks 
substantially the same relief, asking us to order California to sequester the relevant 
ballots and establish a process to verify the citizenship status of those voters before 
counting them. 
II.
At the outset, and given the emergency posture of this case, we assume 
without deciding that the United States possesses both standing and a cause of action
to sue Defendants. Under 28 U.S.C. § 1292(a)(1), we have appellate jurisdiction 
over appeals from interlocutory orders denying injunctive relief. “Ordinarily, we 
lack jurisdiction over the appeal of a TRO.” Newsom v. Trump, 141 F.4th 1032, 1043 
(9th Cir. 2025) (per curiam). But a “denial of a TRO may be appealed if the 
circumstances render the denial tantamount to the denial of a preliminary 
injunction.” Babaria v. Blinken, 87 F.4th 963, 976 (9th Cir. 2023) (citation modified)
(quoting Religious Tech. Ctr., Church of Scientology Int’l, Inc. v. Scott, 869 F.2d 
1306, 1308 (9th Cir. 1989)). To decide that question, we have primarily considered
4a

5
two factors: (1) whether there was a “full adversary hearing” in the district court; 
and (2) whether “in the absence of review, the appellants would be effectively 
foreclosed from pursuing further interlocutory relief.” Scott, 869 F.2d at 1308
(quoting Env’t Def. Fund, Inc. v. Andrus, 625 F.2d 861, 862 (9th Cir. 1980)). We 
have also considered whether “‘the denial of the TRO effectively decided the merits 
of the case’ and rendered plaintiff[’s] claims moot.” Blinken, 87 F.4th at 976 (quoting 
Graham v. Teledyne-Cont’l Motors, 805 F.2d 1386, 1388 (9th Cir. 1986)).
We have jurisdiction over this appeal. First, the district court conducted a 
two-hour “adversary hearing” at which it heard arguments from all parties on the 
merits of the United States’s requested TRO. See Andrus, 625 F.2d at 862. Both the 
United States and Defendants were afforded “notice [and] an opportunity to 
respond,” and both were able to submit briefing and “additional evidence” to the 
district court. Blinken, 87 F.4th at 976; see also Washington v. Trump, 847 F.3d 1151, 
1158 (9th Cir. 2017) (per curiam) (finding appellate jurisdiction where both parties 
“vigorously contested the legal basis for the TRO in written briefs and oral 
arguments before the district court”); Newsom, 141 F.4th at 1043–44 (noting a TRO 
that was “strongly challenged” in the district court is more likely to be “best 
construed as an appealable preliminary injunction” (quoting E. Bay Sanctuary 
Covenant v. Trump, 932 F.3d 742, 762 (9th Cir. 2018)). 
5a

6
In addition, the district court’s order denying the United States’s motion for a 
TRO “effectively foreclosed” the United States “from pursuing further interlocutory 
relief.” Scott, 869 F.2d at 1308 (quoting Andrus, 625 F.2d at 862). In the United 
States’s Complaint, it asked the district court to enjoin California from tabulating 
ballots from voters it had classified as “likely noncitizens in the upcoming federal 
election.” Compl. at 3, No. 26-cv-12025 (C.D. Cal. Oct. 15, 2026), ECF No. 1.3 But
at the adversarial hearing, the district court stated that it did not have the “appropriate 
time” to develop a full record on the relevant “systems” and “algorithms” 
surrounding the veracity of the United States’s list of “likely” noncitizens. TRO 
Hearing Transcript at 93, ECF No. 150. It thus appointed a special master to review 
the United States’s voter roll data and suggested convening another hearing in two 
weeks—well after Election Day on November 3, 2026—to further develop a record
on the issue. Id. at 93–94. And it noted that the purpose of the future hearing would 
be to determine the veracity of the October List, in the event the United States adds 
additional individuals to the list and wishes to bring “indictment[s] against them.” 
Id. at 90. In doing so, the district court in large part rendered the United States’s 
claim—which is ostensibly based on sequestering ballots in the instant election
rather than prosecuting noncitizens afterward—“moot,” or at least moot in 
substantial part because the election is days away. See Blinken, 87 F.4th at 976.
3 All ECF cites refer to the entries in Case No. 26-cv-12025.
6a

7
The “transcript of the hearing and the court’s written order denying the 
application [for a TRO] make it unmistakably clear that the order was tantamount to 
a denial of a preliminary injunction.” Scott, 869 F.2d at 1308. Thus, we have 
appellate jurisdiction and may proceed to the merits. See Newsom, 141 F.4th at 1044.
III.
“The standard for evaluating an injunction pending appeal is similar to that 
employed by district courts in deciding whether to grant a preliminary injunction.” 
Feldman v. Ariz. Sec’y of State’s Off., 843 F.3d 366, 367 (9th Cir. 2016) (en banc). 
The United States “must establish that [it] is likely to succeed on the merits, that [it]
is likely to suffer irreparable harm in the absence of preliminary relief, that the 
balance of equities tips in [its] favor, and that an injunction is in the public interest.” 
Winter v. Nat. Res. Def. Council, Inc., 555 U.S. 7, 20 (2008). 
As to the first factor, which is the most important, Env’t Prot. Info. Ctr. v. 
Carlson, 968 F.3d 985, 989 (9th Cir. 2020), the question is usually whether the 
movant is likely to succeed in arguing on appeal that the district court abused its 
discretion in denying the preliminary injunction, see Brown ex rel. K.M.K. v. Wash.
Interscholastic Activities Ass’n, No. 26-5488, 2026 WL 2891827, at *2 (9th Cir. 
Sept. 25, 2026). “A district court abuses its discretion if it bases its decision on an 
erroneous legal standard or on clearly erroneous factual findings.” Id. (quoting Baird 
v. Bonta, 81 F.4th 1036, 1040 (9th Cir. 2023)). And here, the United States’s burden 
7a

8
is “doubly demanding,” because it seeks a mandatory injunction requiring 
Defendants to segregate ballots that they would not otherwise segregate and to 
affirmatively verify certain voters’ citizenship status before tabulating their vote-bymail ballot. See Garcia v. Google, Inc., 786 F.3d 733, 740 (9th Cir. 2015) (en banc). 
The United States therefore “must establish that the law and facts clearly favor [its] 
position, not simply that [it] is likely to succeed.” Id. 
IV.
A.
We begin with the United States’s likelihood of success on the merits—“the 
most important” of the Winter factors—and whether the “law and facts clearly favor
[its] position, not simply that [it] is likely to succeed.” Garcia, 786 F.3d at 740. The 
United States once again requests that we order Defendants to segregate the ballots 
of alleged noncitizens because, it claims, 18 U.S.C. § 611 preempts California’s
constitutionally permitted statutory scheme adopted by the California legislature. 
But the United States has not made the required showing that such extraordinary 
relief, during an ongoing election, is clearly required by law.
Because this dispute focuses on California’s procedures for administering its 
elections, the Elections Clause of the U.S. Constitution is directly implicated. See
Arizona v. Inter Tribal Council of Arizona, Inc., 570 U.S. 1, 8–9 (2013) (“ITCA”). 
The Elections Clause reads: 
8a

9
The Times, Places and Manner of holding Elections for Senators and 
Representatives, shall be prescribed in each State by the Legislature 
thereof; but the Congress may at any time by Law make or alter such 
Regulations, except as to the Places of chusing Senators. 
U.S. Const. art. I, § 4, cl. 1. This clause expressly dictates which sovereign has the 
authority to prescribe the manner by which congressional elections are conducted. 
Thus, the question remains whether California’s procedures for enforcing election 
requirements, such as the State’s statutory scheme for citizenship-based ballot 
challenges, have been preempted by Congress.
“[T]he [Elections] Clause functions as ‘a default provision; it invests the 
States with responsibility for the mechanics of congressional elections, but only so 
far as Congress declines to pre-empt state legislative choices.’” ITCA, 570 U.S. at 
9 (quoting Foster v. Love, 522 U.S. 67, 69 (1997)). This “broad authority,” Smiley 
v. Holm, 285 U.S. 355, 367 (1932), conferred on states includes the authority over
“notices, registration, supervision of voting, protection of voters, prevention of fraud 
and corrupt practices, counting of votes, [and] duties of inspectors . . . in short, to 
enact the numerous requirements as to procedure and safeguards which . . . are 
necessary in order to enforce the fundamental right involved,” id. at 366. 
Congress, of course, “may supplement these state regulations or may 
substitute its own” because “[i]t has a general supervisory power over the whole 
subject.” Id. at 366–67 (citation modified); ITCA, 570 U.S. at 14 (noting “[t]he 
9a

10
assumption that Congress is reluctant to pre-empt does not hold when Congress acts 
under” the Elections Clause). But Congress’s exercise of its Elections Clause 
preemption power only goes “so far as it is exercised, and no farther.” ITCA, 570 
U.S. at 9 (quoting Ex parte Siebold, 100 U.S. 371, 392 (1880), abrogated on other 
grounds by Glasgow v. Moyer, 225 U.S. 420 (1912)). Indeed, when Congress 
“exercise[s] th[is] power, . . . we are bound to presume that Congress has done so in 
a judicious manner [and] that it has endeavored to guard as far as possible against 
any unnecessary interference with State laws and regulations.” Siebold, 100 U.S. at 
393.
Nothing in § 611, a statute that criminalizes voting by a noncitizen, preempts 
California’s comprehensive statutory scheme that has been duly enacted under the 
Elections Clause. Section 611 provides that:
(a) It shall be unlawful for any alien to vote in any election held solely 
or in part for the purpose of electing a candidate for the office of 
President, Vice President, Presidential elector, Member of the Senate, 
Member of the House of Representatives, Delegate from the District of 
Columbia, or Resident Commissioner, unless–
(1) the election is held partly for some other purpose;
(2) aliens are authorized to vote for such other purpose under a 
State constitution or statute or a local ordinance; and
(3) voting for such other purpose is conducted independently of 
voting for a candidate for such Federal offices, in such a manner 
that an alien has the opportunity to vote for such other purpose, 
10a

11
but not an opportunity to vote for a candidate for any one or more 
of such Federal offices.
(b) Any person who violates this section shall be fined under this title, 
imprisoned not more than one year, or both.
18 U.S.C. § 611(a)–(b). Noticeably absent from the statute is an express preemption 
provision or any language setting forth regulations for how a state deals with 
citizenship challenges to vote-by-mail ballots. Nor is there any provision
authorizing the Department of Justice to take charge of or intervene in a state’s 
administration of an ongoing election.
4
Exercising the power endowed to it by the Constitution, California 
comprehensively administers its elections, including by regulating voter eligibility.
California law, like federal law, plainly prohibits voting by noncitizens. Compare 
18 U.S.C. § 611, with Cal. Const. art. II, § 2(a) (“A United States citizen 18 years of 
age and resident in this State may vote.”). To that end, California has established a 
comprehensive statutory scheme to ensure the integrity of its elections, including by
requiring voter applicants to attest to citizenship under penalty of perjury, requiring 
election officials to match signatures on vote-by-mail ballots to voter registration 
records, and establishing processes for challenging ballots and canceling registration 
4 We do not hold that § 611 could never preempt any state actions or law under the 
Elections Clause, as that broad question is not before us. Instead, we hold only 
that—in this case and under these particular facts—the United States’s attempted use 
of § 611’s preemptive force to obtain the relief it seeks does not align with § 611’s 
text or what § 611 either permits or forbids. 
11a

12
upon sufficient showing of voter ineligibility. See California I, 2026 WL 3212945, 
at *11–12, 19 (Bennett, J., concurring) (detailing California’s statutory scheme on 
citizenship challenges to a voter and vote-by-mail ballots).
If Congress intends to preempt, “state law is preempted by the federal 
election-day statutes only so far as the conflict extends.” Watson v. Republican Nat’l 
Comm., 609 U.S. 672, 697 (2026) (internal quotations omitted); see also Siebold, 
100 U.S. at 392–93 (noting Congress’s power to regulate elections “supersede[s]” 
inconsistent state law “so far as it is exercised, and no farther” and presuming “that 
Congress . . . has endeavored to guard as far as possible against any unnecessary 
interference with State laws and regulations”). But it is unclear (at best) whether 
Congress intended § 611 to have any preemptive effect, much less a preemptive 
effect that forces states to set aside their own state election laws and procedures 
(which, in California’s case, are both detailed and comprehensive) and segregate 
vote-by-mail ballots in a manner inconsistent with those laws and procedures based 
on the Department of Justice’s unsubstantiated allegations that noncitizens may be 
voting. Nothing on the face of § 611 prescribes a process California must follow 
when handling challenged ballots or preempts Defendants’ actions of mailing,
counting, and resolving ballot challenges in accordance with California’s duly 
enacted procedures. See 18 U.S.C. § 611(a)–(b).
12a

13
Because Congress has not exercised the specific power granted to it under the 
Elections Clause to override California’s established laws for challenging ballots or 
removing ineligible voters, the State Legislature’s statutory scheme remains the only 
method to do so. California, and all states, “are given, and in fact, exercise a wide 
discretion in the formulation of a system for the choice by the people of 
representatives in Congress,” see United States v. Classic, 313 U.S. 299, 311 (1941), 
by prescribing a detailed statutory and regulatory scheme, see Moore v. Harper, 600 
U.S. 1, 29 (2023) (“[State l]egislatures must ‘provide a complete code for 
congressional elections,’ including regulations ‘relati[ng] to notices, registration, 
supervision of voting, protection of voters, prevention of fraud and corrupt practices, 
counting of votes, duties of inspectors and canvassers, and making and publication 
of election returns.’” (second alteration in original) (quoting Smiley, 285 U.S. at 
366)). Allowing the United States to misuse § 611 to prescribe how Defendants must 
process ballots would “override the plain and manifest dictates of the Constitution 
itself.” See Siebold, 100 U.S. at 392.
5
 
5 The United States asserts that it is “absur[d] to say that an officer who receives or 
has custody of the ballots given for a representative owes no duty to the national 
government which Congress can enforce.” Siebold, 100 U.S. at 388. But Siebold
dealt with whether Congress had the power to regulate election integrity by
punishing state election officials who commit fraud, not a misdemeanor statute that 
forbids noncitizens voting in federal elections. See id. at 372, 387–88. As explained 
by the Supreme Court, “[the government of the United States] is directly interested 
in the faithful performance, by the officers of election, of their respective duties. 
Those duties are owed as well to the United States as to the State. . . . A violation of 
13a

14
We decline the United States’s invitation to contravene the Elections Clause
by undermining the Constitution’s plain text. See Smiley, 285 U.S. at 365–66 
(recognizing the responsibilities given to states under the Elections Clause); cf.
Dooley v. United States, 183 U.S. 151, 173 (1901) (“The plain language of the 
Constitution should not be made ‘blank paper by construction,’ and its specific 
mandate ought to be obeyed.”). If the United States believes different procedures 
are necessary for vote-by-mail ballots, we believe it should take that suggestion to 
Congress, not the courts. See Watson, 609 U.S. at 695 (“As we have said time and 
again . . . policy arguments are properly directed to legislatures, not courts.”). 
Therefore, we hold the law does not “clearly favor” the United States’s preemption 
argument. See Garcia, 786 F.3d at 740.
Further, the potential violation of the National Voter Registration Act 
(“NVRA”), 52 U.S.C. § 20507(c)(2), provides an independent reason to conclude 
that the United States has not shown a clear likelihood of success. The NVRA 
requires states to “complete, not later than 90 days prior to the date of a primary or 
duty is an offence against the United States, for which the offender is justly amenable 
to that government.” Id. at 388. Because election officials owe a duty to both 
sovereigns, the Court concluded that it would be “almost absur[d] to say that an 
officer who receives or has custody of the ballots . . . owes no duty to the national 
government which Congress can enforce; or that an officer who stuffs the ballot-box 
cannot be made amenable to the United States.” Id. This case is not about state 
election officials convicted of fraud, nor are there allegations that California’s 
election officials were stuffing ballot boxes.
14a

15
general election for Federal office, any program the purpose of which is to 
systematically remove the names of ineligible voters from the official lists of eligible 
voters.” 52 U.S.C. § 20507(c)(2)(A). The United States argues that the NVRA, 
which governs voter registration, does not govern the requested ballot segregation.
But this focus potentially fails to grasp the broader mechanics of California’s 
election code. The United States effectively seeks to cancel (or potentially cancel) 
“batches of registered voters based on a set procedure [which] is systematic as 
opposed to individualized.” Mi Familia Vota v. Fontes, 129 F.4th 691, 716 (9th Cir. 
2025), cert. granted sub nom. Republican Nat’l Comm. v. Mi Familia Vota, 146 S. 
Ct. 2799 (2026). Assuming that the October List provides or generates sufficient 
proof of voter ineligibility, under California law, when the “county elections official” 
receives “proof that [a registered voter] is otherwise ineligible to vote,” the official 
“shall cancel the registration.” Cal. Elec. Code § 2201(a)(8) (emphasis added). So
the consequence of the United States’s request is not merely ballot segregation, but 
ultimately both the cancellation of the ballot and the removal of voters from the 
voting rolls. 
To be sure, as we have recognized, “the plain language of the 90-day Provision 
lets states continue any non-systematic cancellation of registrations within the 90-
day window.” Mi Familia Vota, 129 F.4th at 716. Indeed, Congress permitted such 
individualized cancellations but prohibited systematic ones “because such programs 
15a

16
can cause inaccurate removal and ‘[e]ligible voters removed days or weeks before 
Election Day will likely not be able to correct the State’s errors in time to vote.’” Id.
(alteration in original) (citing Arcia v. Fla. Sec’y of State, 772 F.3d 1335, 1346 (11th 
Cir. 2014)).
Such “rigorous individualized inquiry[] lead[s] to a smaller chance for 
mistakes.” Id. But the United States seeks to challenge an entire batch of 20,000 
ballots. In the district court’s view, “Plaintiff’s protocol raises significant concerns.”
For example, the district court determined that the United States “provided ‘no error 
rates’ or ‘validation against a reliable benchmark’ that would enable a determination 
of the accuracy of its findings.” The district court also found that the United States
did not provide any information on how the data enhancement was conducted—“It 
remains unknown how Lexis Nexis performed its analysis, such as how it ‘linked 
names to Social Security numbers not available on the California public voter file.’” 
The suspect reliability of these lists found by the district court reflects the concern 
Congress sought to mitigate with the 90-day quiet period. This adds to our reasons 
for finding that overall, the district court did not abuse its discretion in refusing to 
grant the United States’s proposed injunction, as the United States did not clearly 
show the NVRA permits its desired relief. 
B.
16a

17
The United States also fails to demonstrate that it will likely, let alone clearly,
suffer irreparable harm. See Garcia, 786 F.3d at 740. Because the United States’s
preemption argument is likely unavailing, it follows that any resulting harm is also 
unlikely. Cf. Hale v. Dep’t of Energy, 806 F.2d 910, 918 (9th Cir. 1986) (“Absent a 
First Amendment claim, the appellants have failed to establish that irreparable harm 
will flow from a failure to preliminarily enjoin defendants’ actions.”). The district 
court also found that the United States’s process in creating the October List was not 
credible, and thus the United States’s assertion that individuals on the October List 
are “highly likely to be noncitizens” is also not credible.6 That finding, along with 
California’s established procedures for ensuring voter eligibility, substantially 
weaken the United States’s claim that it is likely to suffer irreparable harm from 
ballots being cast by noncitizens.
The balance of hardships and the public interest also do not weigh in the 
United States’s favor. Major concerns remain that granting the United States’s
requested relief might result in immense hardship to Defendants and harm the public 
interest by risking the disenfranchisement of eligible voters and putting the entire 
tabulation process in jeopardy. The district court found that the United States’s 
“request for election officials to identify and segregate ballots belonging to 
6 The United States challenges the district court’s findings. But it fails to show any 
clear error given the conflicting evidence in the record. See Baird v. Bonta, 81 F.4th 
1036, 1040 (9th Cir. 2023).
17a

18
individuals on the October List would force Defendants to create wholly new 
procedures while the election is already underway.” Crediting the declaration of the 
County’s Assistant Registrar of the Information Technology Bureau, the district 
court stated that the scale of the required technological changes to California’s voter 
system “cannot be completed safely and uniformly before Election Day,” and could 
result in a failure of the County’s central election management system, “jeopardizing 
the Secretary’s ability to meet the election certification deadline of December 11.”
As a result, the district court found that “granting [the United States]’s request would 
provoke catastrophic change, upending the administration of the election. This 
would likely cause ‘voter confusion and consequent incentive to remain away from 
the polls’ as individuals would wonder whether their ballots were likely to be 
withheld.” (quoting Purcell v. Gonzalez, 549 U.S. 1, 4–5 (2006)).7
To be sure, there are countervailing public interests at stake. There is a public 
interest in maintaining the integrity of elections. But as discussed, the district court 
found that the risks that noncitizens are voting are, at best, uncertain, and also 
7 There were conflicting declarations on the potential burden that would result from 
granting the United States’s requested relief. But the district court reasonably 
credited the declaration of the County’s Assistant Registrar of the Information 
Technology Bureau, who is presumably informed about the inner workings of the 
County’s electronic voter system, over the declaration from an elected Registrar 
from a different county. The district court certainly did not abuse its discretion in 
this regard.
18a

19
tempered by California’s established voter-eligibility procedures. In contrast, there 
is a material risk that granting the United States its requested relief would result in 
disenfranchisement and could jeopardize the County’s entire election. Thus, the 
balance of hardships and the public interest weigh in Defendants’ favor.
Finally, Purcell counsels that we should not intervene at this late hour. The 
Purcell principle reflects the wisdom that we must not “alter the election rules on 
the eve of an election.” Republican Nat’l Comm. v. Democratic Nat’l Comm., 589 
U.S. 423, 424 (2020) (per curiam). “The Purcell principle applies with even greater 
force” when, as here, an election is already underway. People Not Politicians v. 
Onder, No. 26A388, 2026 WL 2883222, at *2 (U.S. Sept. 25, 2026) (per curiam);
see California I, 2026 WL 3212945, at *18 (Sanchez, J., concurring) (explaining that 
“it is not only voter confusion that matters in the Purcell analysis but election 
administration and broader electoral disorder stemming from late federal courtordered changes to election rules”). Just this year, the Supreme Court emphasized 
that “late-breaking, court-ordered rule changes,” such as those the United States 
requests, “can ‘result in voter confusion and consequent incentive to remain away 
from the polls,’ and thus undermine the ‘[c]onfidence in the integrity of our electoral 
processes . . . essential to the functioning of our participatory democracy.’” Bost v. 
Ill. State Bd. of Elections, 607 U.S. 71, 80 (2026) (quoting Purcell, 549 U.S. at 4–
5)). 
19a

20
Defendants, pursuant to their constitutional authority, established rules and 
procedures to challenge a voter’s ineligibility in the months directly preceding an 
election. And the United States’s requested relief is simple only in the abstract. As 
the district court found—and we discern no clear error—there is no feasible way to 
identify and segregate the ballots of specific individuals without potentially 
catastrophic effects on the entire system.
8
The United States contends there is no Purcell problem, relying in part on
Republican Party of Pennsylvania v. Boockvar, No. 20A84, 2020 WL 6536912, at 
*1 (Mem) (U.S. Nov. 6, 2020). The comparison is inapt. In Boockvar, 
Pennsylvania’s Secretary of the Commonwealth had ordered county boards of 
elections to segregate ballots received by mail within three days of election night. 
Id. Justice Alito issued an interim order merely commanding electoral officials “to 
comply with the [Secretary’s] . . . guidance.” Id. The segregation process, therefore, 
followed existing state guidance and was markedly simpler than the injunction 
requested by the United States. As the district court found, “[b]ecause the county 
Registrar’s current system ‘ha[s] no function for setting aside the ballots of 
designated voters,’ complying with [the United States’s] request would require 
8
Indeed, the declaration of the County’s Assistant Registrar of the Information 
Technology Bureau states: “[B]ased on my technical expertise, I have grave 
concerns about the potential catastrophic impact of implementing the DOJ’s request 
to ‘set aside vote-by-mail ballots from persons identified by the Federal Government 
likely to be noncitizens’ based on a list of approximately 20,000 individuals . . . .”
20a

I. 
Section 611(a) Is an Elections Clause Statute
Congress “may at any time . . . make or alter” state regulations dealing with 
the “Times, Places and Manner of holding Elections for Senators and 
Representatives.” U.S. Const. art. I, § 4, cl. 1. “What is the plain meaning of these 
words? . . . [W]e should not have any difficulty in understanding them.” Ex parte

Siebold, 100 U.S. at 383. In fact, the meaning is obvious: While States set the initial 
rules in federal elections, Congress gets the final word. 
The Elections Clause empowers Congress to safeguard federal elections. 
Congress can exercise that authority “not only as to times and places, but [also] in 
relation to notices, registration, supervision of voting, protection of voters, 
prevention of fraud and corrupt practices, counting of votes, duties of inspectors and 
canvassers, and making and publication of election returns.” Smiley v. Holm, 285 
U.S. 355, 366 (1932). Thus, its power extends to innumerable “requirements as to 
procedure and safeguards” necessary to protect the integrity of federal elections. Id.
That power may also take the form of criminal sanctions. In 1870, Congress 
passed a criminal statute providing federal penalties for the violation of state election 
law. See Enforcement Act of 1870, ch. 114, 16 Stat. 140. Soon after, in Ex parte 
Siebold, five Maryland officials challenged the constitutionality of the Act, which 
supplemented Maryland’s criminal election laws. 100 U.S. at 374, 380. The officials 
violated state law in many ways, including by stuffing the ballot box and refusing to 
let federal officials observe vote counting. Id. at 378–79. The Supreme Court held 
that the Enforcement Act was a valid exercise of the Elections Clause. Id. at 383–
84; see also United States v. Classic, 313 U.S. 299, 321–23 (1941) (recognizing that 
Congress may criminalize interference with the right to vote once a State has

conferred the right). Even though the state officials violated state law, federal law 
could impose criminal liability for that same conduct.
The Enforcement Act also made it a felony to cast a ballot “without having a 
lawful right to vote” in federal elections. Enforcement Act of 1870, ch. 114, § 19, 
16 Stat. 140, 144. While States decided which persons had the right to vote, 
Congress reinforced these preferences with criminal sanctions. See Ex parte 
Siebold, 100 U.S. at 388 (“[Congress] has only created additional sanctions for their 
performance, and provided means of supervision in order more effectually to secure 
such performance.”). The fact that Congress’s “Times, Places and Manner” 
authority supplemented state law made no difference because “no repugnance in the 
system of regulations can arise thence; for the power of Congress over the subject is 
paramount.” Id. at 383–84; see also Ex parte Coy, 127 U.S. 731, 761 (1888) (Field, 
J., dissenting) (observing that “Congress had the power under the constitution to 
adopt the laws of the states respecting [congressional] election[s] . . . and that it 
could impose a punishment for a violation of such laws”). That follows from the 
plain meaning of the Clause—Congress can protect the “Manner” of federal 
elections in any way it sees fit.
In that vein, Congress passed § 611(a) against the backdrop of longstanding 
bans against alien voting. While suffrage is critically important, States regulate who 
may vote in elections. Cf. Minor v. Happersett, 88 U.S. (21 Wall.) 162, 178 (1874).

laws of the United States on the subject of naturalization.” Wis. Const. art. III, § 1

vote. Arkansas became the last state to end this “political anomaly[,] . . . doubtless 
never to return.” Leon E. Aylsworth, The Passing of Alien Suffrage, 25 Am. Pol.

Once we understand that federal law preempts state action, the remedy 
typically involves enjoining that state action. And as a matter of history, federal 
intervention in the state administration of elections is commonplace. So ordering 
California to stop commingling illegal ballots is a straightforward application of our 
equitable powers.

action or policy preempted by federal law. See, e.g., United States v. Alaska, No. 22-

Federal courts have a “virtually unflagging” duty to uphold the law. Lexmark

preempted under § 611(a) and enjoin California from commingling its ballots

The federal government and the States can work together. California decided

seeks to safeguard that decision. We should have let them try.

I. INTRODUCTION 
This case is about the right of every American citizen to vote in a free and fair election. 
Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, 
sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections 
procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch. In bringing this lawsuit, the Executive 
would have this Court believe that it reigns as a sole sovereign. But California and its people 
are sovereign, too. 
The right to vote has long been understood as integral to both citizenship and 
participation in our democracy. Ronald Reagan described this right as “the crown jewel of 
American liberties, and we will not see its luster diminished.” Remarks on Signing the Voting 
Rights Act Amendments of 1982 (June 19, 1982) (extending the Voting Rights Act of 1965). 
But access to voting has always been contested. At the inception of our country, African 
Americans and women of all ethnicities were denied access to the ballot. Their push to be 
recognized as equal citizens of this nation led to the Fifteenth Amendment in 1870 and the 
Nineteenth Amendment in 1920, which declared that the right to vote could not be denied due 
to someone’s race or gender. But these amendments did not guarantee all citizens’ 
enfranchisement in practice. Minority communities continued to fight for suffrage. Poll taxes, 
literacy tests, and other obstacles were further used to prevent individuals from casting their 
vote. 
Every generation in our history has witnessed repeated clashes between those who seek 
to limit access to the ballot and those who fight to ensure it. In this case, the federal government 
seeks to segregate and exclude over 20,000 ballots. This request violates longstanding 
constitutional principles mandating that states have control over their elections. If Plaintiff’s 
last-minute request for relief were granted, either party could create chaos for their own 
political purposes to disrupt the election process. Over 20,000 registered Californians would 
potentially lose the right that generations of Americans have fought to preserve.

We start, as we must, with jurisdiction. See HayDay Farms, Inc. v. FeeDx

A.
Under 28 U.S.C. § 1292(a)(1), we have jurisdiction over appeals from 
“[i]nterlocutory orders of the district courts of the United States . . . granting, 
continuing, modifying, refusing or dissolving injunctions, or refusing to dissolve or 
modify injunctions, except where a direct review may be had in the Supreme Court.” 
28 U.S.C. § 1292(a)(1). Thus, in the normal course, whenever a district court denies 
a preliminary injunction, that denial is an appealable interlocutory order. Id. 
But we also have jurisdiction over interlocutory appeals in which “the district 
court effectively denied the motion” for injunctive relief. Mt. Graham Red Squirrel 
v. Madigan, 954 F.2d 1441, 1449–50 (9th Cir. 1992). This is because, since 
“preliminary relief must be granted promptly to be effective, simple inaction may

II.
To obtain preliminary injunctive relief, a plaintiff “must establish that [it] is 
likely to succeed on the merits, that [it] is likely to suffer irreparable harm in the 
absence of preliminary relief, that the balance of equities tips in [its] favor, and that 
an injunction is in the public interest.” Winter v. Nat. Res. Def. Council, Inc., 555 
U.S. 7, 20 (2008). Plaintiff argues that it needs an injunction to maintain the status 
quo, and that its proposed injunction does no more than maintain the status quo. I 
disagree. Because Plaintiff urges this court to require Defendants to take 
“affirmative action”—to segregate California’s ballots that the State would not 
otherwise segregate and to affirmatively verify certain voters’ citizenship status 
before tabulating their vote-by-mail ballot—Plaintiff requests a mandatory 
injunction. See Garcia v. Google, Inc., 786 F.3d 733, 740 (9th Cir. 2015) (en banc). 
“The standard for issuing a mandatory preliminary injunction is high.” Doe 
v. Snyder, 28 F.4th 103, 111 (9th Cir. 2022). “In general, mandatory injunctions ‘are 
not granted unless extreme or very serious damage will result and are not issued in

GmbH & Co., 571 F.3d 873, 879 (9th Cir. 2009)). The movant “must establish that 
the law and facts clearly favor [its] position, not simply that [it] is likely to succeed.” 
Garcia, 786 F.3d at 740. And in deciding to grant equitable relief, the remedy must 
be workable. North Carolina v. Covington, 581 U.S. 486, 488 (2017) (per curiam)
(quotation marks omitted) (quoting New York v. Cathedral Acad., 434 U.S. 125, 129 
(1977)). In my view, Plaintiff fails to meet these heightened standards. 
A.

“the most important” of the Winter factors—and whether the “law and facts clearly 
favor [its] position, not simply that [it] is likely to succeed.” Garcia, 786 F.3d at 
740. Plaintiff asks this court—in an expedited and preliminary posture—to order 
Defendants to segregate the ballots of alleged noncitizens because, it argues, 18 
U.S.C. § 611 preempts California’s declination and preempts California from 
following the statutory scheme adopted by the California Legislature. Yet Plaintiff 
has not made the required showing that such extraordinary relief, in the days leading 
up to an election, is clearly required by law.
As an initial matter, there is no dispute that it is unlawful under both federal 
and California law for noncitizens to vote. Compare 18 U.S.C. § 611, with Cal.

prohibition, which plainly implicates the Elections Clause of the U.S. Constitution. 
See Arizona v. Inter Tribal Council of Arizona, Inc., 570 U.S. 1, 8–9 (2013) 
(“ITCA”). The Elections Clause, U.S. Const. art. I, § 4, cl. 1, reads: 
The Times, Places and Manner of holding Elections for Senators and 
Representatives, shall be prescribed in each State by the Legislature 
thereof; but the Congress may at any time by Law make or alter such 
Regulations, except as to the Places of chusing Senators. 
This clause expressly dictates which sovereign has the authority to prescribe the 
manner by which Congressional elections are conducted. The question therefore is 
whether Congress has spoken clearly—that is, whether California’s procedures in 
enforcing the election requirements, such as citizenship or ballot challenges based 
on citizenship, have been preempted. Nothing in § 611—a statute that criminalizes 
voting by a noncitizen—preempts California’s comprehensive statutory scheme that 
has been duly enacted under the Elections Clause. 
While Plaintiff argues that the Supremacy Clause requires California to 
segregate several thousand ballots because failing to do so would at a minimum 
“induce, encourage or promote” the violation of § 611, this court has recognized that
“the Elections Clause operates quite differently from the Supremacy Clause.” 
Gonzalez v. Arizona, 677 F.3d 383, 391 (9th Cir. 2012) (en banc), aff’d sub nom. 
Arizona v. Inter Tribal Council of Arizona, Inc., 570 U.S. 1 (2013). “In practice, the 
[Elections] Clause functions as ‘a default provision; it invests the States with

notices, registration, supervision of voting, protection of voters, 
prevention of fraud and corrupt practices, counting of votes, duties of

likely to succeed on the merits because Plaintiff has not shown that the law clearly 
favors its position. First, § 611 does what each party has determined is unlawful—

B. 
No Purcell Voter Confusion
The Purcell principle is a well-known safeguard against “[l]ate judicial 
tinkering with election laws.” Merrill v. Milligan, 142 S. Ct. 879, 881 (2022) 
(Kavanaugh, J., concurring). But the “principle . . . is not absolute.” Id. It’s 
prudential, and courts may consider the merits of the plaintiff’s claim, whether the 
plaintiff will suffer irreparable harm without an injunction, whether the plaintiff 
“unduly delayed” in bringing the complaint, and whether the proposed changes “are 
at least feasible.” Id. 
So the doctrine does not immediately apply to all election-related cases. 
Instead, it stems from the commonsense observation that “[c]ourt orders affecting 
elections, especially conflicting orders, can . . . result in voter confusion and 
consequent incentive to remain away from the polls.” Purcell, 549 U.S. at 4–5. 
Voters need to know “the rules of the road”: “how, when, and where” to vote. 
Democratic Nat’l Comm. v. Wis. State Legislature, 592 U.S. 1039, 1043 (2020)
(Kavanaugh, J., concurring). 
But here, whether state officials commingle ballots that have already been 
submitted can’t possibly cause voter confusion about how, when, or where to vote—

California lastly asserts that the NVRA prevents it from cooperating with the 
federal government. The NVRA implements a 90-day “quiet period” before an 
election, during which a State cannot carry out a “program” of removing ineligible

VIII. 
CONCLUSION
The federal government came to us for help as it sought to enforce Congress’s 
law against illegal voting by aliens. It did so because California would not help. 
Instead, California interpreted state and federal law to stop it from doing so, while
empowering it to mix legal and likely illegal ballots together. Because the State
frustrates federal law by relying on that interpretation to commingle ballots, its 
actions are preempted. We should’ve stopped it from doing so and effectuated 
Congress’s will. I respectfully dissent.
